questions.text: Let \(S_T\) be the spot price of an asset at maturity \(T\) and \(K\) be the delivery price of a forward contract. Derive the profit function for a long position in this forward contract. Prove algebraically that the potential gain is unbounded while the maximum loss is strictly bounded, setting up the profit function as: \[ \Pi = S_T - K \]

Derive the profit function for a short forward contract with delivery price \(K\) and spot price at maturity \(S_T\). Prove that the maximum possible profit is bounded by \(K\), assuming the asset price cannot be negative, by evaluating the expression: \[ \Pi = K - S_T \]

Prove algebraically that a forward contract traded between Party A (long) and Party B (short) is a zero-sum game. Use \(S_T\) for the spot price at maturity and \(K\) for the delivery price, showing that the sum of their payoffs equals zero by evaluating: \[ \Pi_{total} = (S_T - K) + (K - S_T) \]

An investor buys a European call option with strike price \(K\) for a premium \(c\). Derive the break-even spot price \(S_T\) at maturity by solving: \[ \max(S_T - K, 0) - c = 0 \] Prove mathematically that the maximum loss is exactly \(c\).

Derive the break-even spot price \(S_T\) at maturity for a short European put option with strike \(K\) and premium \(p\). Solve the equation: \[ p - \max(K - S_T, 0) = 0 \] and mathematically prove the maximum possible loss for the option writer.

An investor wants to take a long position. The spot price of an asset is \(S_0\) and the initial margin for a futures contract of size \(M\) is \(I\), where \(I < M \cdot S_0\). Derive the expression for the leverage ratio \(L\) achieved by using futures instead of the spot market: \[ L = \frac{M \cdot S_0}{I} \]

The spot price of gold is \(S_0\) and the 1-year forward price is \(F_0\). The 1-year borrowing rate is \(r\). If the forward price exceeds the future value of the spot price such that \[ F_0 > S_0(1+r) \] derive the step-by-step cash flows of an arbitrage strategy to prove a risk-free profit can be locked in today.

Assume a stock price is \(S_0\) and its 1-year forward price is \(F_0\). The 1-year risk-free lending rate is \(r\). If the forward price is too low, such that \[ F_0 < S_0(1+r) \] derive the arbitrage proof showing how an investor already owning the stock can increase their 1-year yield without taking additional risk.

Derive the mathematical difference in payoffs at maturity \(T\) between a long forward contract with delivery price \(K\) and a long European call option with strike price \(K\). Evaluate the difference: \[ \Delta = \max(S_T - K, 0) - (S_T - K) \] and prove under what condition the call strictly outperforms the forward.

A company owns \(N\) shares of a stock currently priced at \(S_0\). They buy \(N\) put options with strike \(K\) and premium \(p\). Derive the minimum guaranteed portfolio value at maturity \(T\) by analyzing the combined payoff: \[ V_T = N \cdot S_T + N \cdot \max(K - S_T, 0) \]

An exporter will receive \(X\) units of foreign currency at time \(T\). The current forward exchange rate is \(F_0\). Derive the exact domestic currency cash flow at time \(T\) if the exporter hedges using a forward contract. Prove that the variance of the hedged cash flow is zero, given: \[ \text{Cash Flow} = X \cdot F_0 \]

A trader holds a long forward contract with delivery price \(K\) and buys a European put option with strike price \(K\) and premium \(p\). Derive the net payoff function at maturity \(T\) and prove that it is equivalent to a long European call option payoff by evaluating: \[ (S_T - K) + \max(K - S_T, 0) \]

An investor buys a stock at \(S_0\) and writes a European call option with strike \(K\) for premium \(c\). Derive the overall profit function at maturity \(T\) as a function of the final stock price \(S_T\) by simplifying: \[ \Pi = (S_T - S_0) + c - \max(S_T - K, 0) \] Prove the maximum possible profit.

A stock trades at \(P_A\) in Market A and \(P_B\) in Market B. The exchange rate is \(E\) (units of B per unit of A). If the price in Market B exceeds the converted price from Market A, such that \[ P_B > P_A \cdot E \] derive the algebraic proof of the arbitrage profit per share, detailing the simultaneous trades required.

A structured bond pays a principal of 1000 plus an additional amount based on the price of oil \(S_T\) at maturity. The additional amount is \(170 \max(S_T - 25, 0)\), capped at a maximum of 2550. Prove algebraically that this payoff can be decomposed by setting up the equivalence: \[ \text{Payoff} = 1000 + 170 \max(S_T - 25, 0) - 170 \max(S_T - 40, 0) \]

Prove that selling a European put option with strike \(K\) for a premium \(p\) has a bounded payoff profile. Derive the maximum profit and maximum loss from the profit function: \[ \Pi = p - \max(K - S_T, 0) \]

An investor shorts a forward contract on \(N\) units of foreign exchange at rate \(F_0\). Derive the profit function if the spot rate at maturity is \(S_T\). Prove that the profit is strictly positive if \(S_T < F_0\) using the relationship: \[ \Pi = N(F_0 - S_T) \]

Derive the mathematical difference in terminal profit between shorting a stock at \(S_0\) and buying a European put option with strike \(K = S_0\) for premium \(p\). Evaluate the difference: \[ \Delta = (S_0 - S_T) - (\max(S_0 - S_T, 0) - p) \] Prove which strategy has unbounded downside risk.

Derive the profit function for a European call option on a stock with strike \(K_1\) and premium \(c\), and a European put on the same stock with strike \(K_2\) and premium \(p\), where \(K_1 < K_2\). Prove that the terminal payoff before premiums is always strictly positive: \[ \text{Payoff} = \max(S_T - K_1, 0) + \max(K_2 - S_T, 0) > 0 \]

Derive the net profit of buying 100 shares at \(S_0\) and buying 100 put options with strike \(K\) for premium \(p\). Prove that the downside risk is entirely eliminated for \(S_T < K\) by calculating the derivative of the profit function with respect to \(S_T\): \[ \frac{d\Pi}{dS_T} = 0 \]
